# What does the portal tell me?

*You'll need PnL as cash plus position (chapter 2), the rehearsals (chapter 1) and a backtest's assumptions
(chapter 10).*

## The story

In the Varde rehearsal, the fourth disguised round we ran before the event, the first upload scored €367.61 on the
three public sessions. Before the order fee, which our engine can't charge, the portal's gross was €511; our backtest of the same file, under
its best reading of the exchange's rules, had said about €1,330 [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/DRYRUN_LOG.md`)]{.src}.
And calibrate, the tool that searches our engine's settings for one that reproduces the portal, refused: no
setting came within 5% of every figure (@fig-calibrate).

So the session read the portal's results file by hand. The rules had said there was a fee per order placed as well as
per lot, and it was easy to underrate: the bot placed and cancelled orders all the time, 28,647 of them, and at half a
cent each they took €143.24 of a €510.85 gross, **28%**
[(`data/sessions.csv`; `python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/DRYRUN_LOG.md`, "What calibrate printed")]{.src}.
The fills showed a second gap: the portal had filled far fewer lots than any of our settings that traded at all, 8,466
against 11,345 to 18,772. The rule behind it, that only half of each print reached resting orders, was not in the rules
the session had; it sat in the rehearsal's answer key [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/README.md`)]{.src}.

The first rehearsal had taught the same lesson from the other side. Its bot made 42,446 in that round's units on the
hidden days, replayed the usual way, with the recorded book restored every step. With what it took kept gone from
the book, it made 31,172: **27% less**, from one assumption about the exchange and nothing in the strategy
[(`data/depletion.csv`, from `python/experiments/mock_round/private/evaluate.py ... --days hidden [--deplete]`)]{.src}.

Neither gap was a strategy problem, and either would have misled every backtest that night. The portal's figures were
the only place they showed.

## The idea

### The twelve figures

An upload comes back with a dozen numbers. On the Arena's portal they have these names
[(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Known so far")]{.src}; the Varde rehearsal's portal reported the same ones, and its upload gave:

| Figure | Varde upload | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `score` | 367.61 | the PnL that ranks you: on the Varde portal, cash plus the positions at the mark, less any penalty (inferred for the Arena) |
| `fills`, `tradedVolume` | 5,056; 8,466 | how many fills, and how many lots |
| `inventory` | −6 | the last session's end position, summed over products |
| `cash` | 2,310.30 | cash at the end, fees included |
| `markPrice` | 233.44 | the last session's marks, averaged over products |
| `breachPenalty` | 0 | the charge for going past a limit |
| `pnlSe` | 22.98 | the score's standard error |
| `absInventoryQ50` to `Q997` | 8, 13, 27, 36 | quantiles of the absolute position, pooled over the sessions |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
The Varde upload came back with a score of 367.61 euros, 5,056 fills over 8,466 lots, an end position of minus 6, cash
of 2,310 euros, a mark price of 233.44 euros, no penalty, a standard error of 22.98 euros, and an absolute position of 8 lots
at the median, 13 at the 68th percentile, 27 at the 95th and 36 at the 99.7th.
:::

[(`data/portal_metrics.csv`, from the rehearsal's `portal.py`)]{.src} Four of them repay a closer look.

### The score is an identity, if you know what is summed

It is cash plus position times mark, less any penalty, as in chapter 2, and you can check it. With one product and one
session the check is exact. On the Varde upload it fails twice over, and nothing is wrong: `cash` is summed over all
three sessions while `inventory` and `markPrice` are the last session's, and `markPrice` is one number averaged over
three products' prices, one of which the bot never traded. So 2,310.30 less 6 times 233.44 is not 367.61; the identity
holds only session by session and product by product (chapter 2 draws the parts). The session
rebuilt the score from the results file, valuing each session's end position at its last mid, and got €369.67 against
the portal's 367.61, within 0.6%: the score was the *sum* over the sessions, not their mean
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/DRYRUN_LOG.md`)]{.src}.

That rebuild is the first of four checks the day's question file asks of the first upload: the identity; the whole path
(fills, volume, end position and the position quantiles, not just PnL); the aggregation (is `score` a sum or a mean,
and which standard error is `pnlSe`); and the clock (one continuous run, or a reset per day)
[(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "How is PnL scored?")]{.src}. Know which figures are sums before you compare any of them.

### The standard error says how much the score is worth

On the Varde portal it is the standard error of the total over the sessions scored
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/private/portal.py`)]{.src}:

::: {.eq speak="the standard error of a total over n sessions is the spread of the session scores times the square root of n"}
$$\text{pnlSe} = \text{sd}(\text{session scores}) \times \sqrt{n}$$
:::

The Varde sessions scored 110.21, 136.57 and 120.83 euros: their spread is 13.3, times the square root of 3 is 23
[(`data/sessions.csv`)]{.src}. Two uploads whose scores differ by less than a couple of standard errors are not shown to
differ, however tempting the better number. With a handful of uploads a round, this is what stops you chasing noise.
RUNBOOK has a second, separate bar: the engine's error, the gap between an upload's portal score and our backtest of it,
measured by T+2:00, and never to choose between two variants by a portal score that
differs by less than that [(`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round" and "Rules that hold all day")]{.src}. One is the portal's own
noise, the other our simulator's distance from it.

The Arena's portal shows a `pnlSe` too, but what it measures isn't known: it could be over sessions, over blocks of
one run, or over repeated runs of a noisy simulation. So `arena.backtest` with `--metrics` prints our engine's version of every
figure, with guesses at the standard error (ticks taken as independent, 20 blocks' sums, and, over several days, the
daily PnLs' spread times the square root of the days), and calibrate tries
per-tick, per-block and per-day versions and keeps the one that fits
[(`python/arena/report.py`, `format_metrics_total`; `python/experiments/day/calibrate.py`; `ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Probes", 16)]{.src}. One more thing can set the noise floor:
Prosperity 4's portal scored each upload on a random 80% of the quotes, drawn again every time, so two uploads of
one file differed [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Known so far")]{.src}. If the Arena does that, the gap between two uploads of the
same file is the smallest difference worth believing.

### The position quantiles say how hard the bot leans on its limits

The quantiles pool the absolute position over the sessions, summed over products, and the two products the Varde bot
traded allowed 100 lots between them. A median of 8 lots and a 99.7th percentile of 36 mean the bot was usually near
flat, and all but 0.3% of the time used at most about a third of its room. A bot whose median sits near its limit is carrying a bet, whether it
meant to or not, and chapter 6 says what that costs. The quantiles are also the cheapest check of the whole path: a
backtest that matches the score but not the quantiles reached the right number by a different route.

### Calibrate: fitting the simulator to the real thing

Our backtest has a dozen settings that recorded data can't decide (chapter 10): which prints fill us, whether orders
rest and where they queue, delay, depletion, the mark, the share of each print we can get, fees and caps. One upload of
a plain bot measures them. Calibrate replays the uploaded file under every combination, 144 settings and more, delay 0
and 1 among them, computes the same twelve figures for each, and ranks the settings by their *worst* figure's error
against the portal. If the best is within 5% on every figure, it prints the settings to paste into the day's format
plug-in, and lists the settings this upload can't tell apart (every figure within 0.5% of each other), which the probes
must decide. If not, it refuses, and names the usual causes: the money off by one factor (a unit or scale mismatch), a
cost the engine doesn't charge, or our wrapper doing something their exchange doesn't
[(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "How is PnL scored?")]{.src}.

![Calibrate on the Varde upload: each figure's error, for the best-ranked setting and for the setting closest on fills
and volume alone, against calibrate's 5% line. Data: `data/calibrate.csv`, from `experiments.day.calibrate` through the
round's plug-in.](../figures/f12_calibrate.png){#fig-calibrate
fig-alt="Dot plot of the error on eleven of the twelve figures (the penalty, zero on both sides, isn't drawn). The best-ranked setting is near 100% off on score, fills and volume. The setting closest on the fills is 2.6% off on fills and 10.5% on volume but 36% off on the score and over 300% on cash. Only the mark price is within 5% for both."}

@fig-calibrate shows why it refused. The best-ranked setting, `none` with a one-tick delay, barely trades: it scores €7,
which makes it "least wrong" on cash and inventory and 98% wrong on the score. The setting closest on fills and volume,
resting with half of each print available, gets fills within 2.6%, but it scores €236.58 against the portal's €367.61
and ends the last session at −12 lots against −6, which throws cash off by over 300%
[(`data/calibrate.csv`)]{.src}. On top of that, the order fee is a cost the engine can't charge at all. No setting can
be right everywhere when the exchange has rules the engine lacks.

### Refusing a bad fit

The refusal was the most useful thing calibrate did that night. A fit that is right on some figures and wrong on
others would have been worse than none: pasted into the plug-in, it would have tuned every later grid to an exchange
that doesn't exist. The session did what the refusal says: it pasted no settings, kept the rules' own, widened the
grid's modes to `all`, `worse` and `none` with a one-tick delay as a scenario, and read every local PnL net of the
order fee. And it wrote down the scale of the gap: the local backtest overstated the portal about 2.6 times on gross
(€1,332 against €511 over the three sessions), so until the next upload a local figure was a ranking, not a forecast
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/DRYRUN_LOG.md`)]{.src}.

That last distinction is the one to keep. A biased simulator can still rank two variants correctly if the bias hits
both alike; the fill model of chapter 10 is the case where it doesn't, because the bias depends on the parameter being
tuned. So a refusal changes how a backtest is read, not whether it is used: every comparison under two or three fill
models, and the portal's score, when it comes, as the judge.

When a gap remains, `experiments.day.shortfall` splits it per order: the same lots at a lower edge mean later or worse
fills (try `--delay 1`); fewer lots mean the fill model differs, as on Varde, and depletion is the other candidate
the first rehearsal named [(`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "How is PnL scored?"; `IDEAS.md`, "Implementation shortfall and missed-trade cost per order")]{.src}.

::: {.callout-note title="What would differ on another market"}
On Prosperity, the open-source backtester follows the platform's published matching, and the gaps teams reported were
the fill question of chapter 10 (Kayzerjali's +2,415 against +436 on one window, *their claim*). On ABIDES the simulator is the
market, so calibrate has nothing to do. On the Varde rehearsal the gap was a hidden fee and a hidden fill rule, and
calibrate's job was to notice. The Arena's portal is the first real target, and what its `pnlSe` and `markPrice` mean is
unknown until its first upload.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Calibrate is system identification: fit a simulator's parameters so that its outputs match logs from the real system.
Two things limit it, and they are where the analogy to an ordinary fit breaks. It sees twelve aggregate figures, not
the hidden state, so very different settings can match the same totals; that is why it ranks by the worst figure, not
the average, and why it lists the settings it can't separate. And the simulator's family may not contain the truth:
refusing a bad fit is the same discipline as not deploying a model whose validation loss says it doesn't fit, however
good its best metric looks. A misspecified model fitted anyway gives confident, wrong parameters.
:::
